analysis.one_liner: Lets former students refinance federal and private student loans at today's lower rates, paid for by a minimum tax on millionaires.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote in the Senate; it died in committee, so no student loans were refinanced and the tax on high incomes never took effect.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let people with older federal student loans — including bank-issued FFEL loans — and some private student loans refinance them at the lower interest rates that applied to new federal loans for the school year starting July 1, 2013, with the new rate fixed for the life of the loan. Eligibility would be based on income or debt-to-income, prioritizing borrowers in the greatest financial need. To pay for it, the bill imposed a new 30% minimum tax on each dollar of income above $1 million, and the refinancing program would shut down once its cost used up the revenue that tax raised.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers holding federal student loans taken out before July 2013 — when interest rates on new loans were substantially higher — plus qualified borrowers carrying private student loans. Both groups could cut their interest rate to the lower 2013–14 federal rate and keep it for the life of the loan, reducing monthly payments and total interest paid. Eligibility rules would steer the benefit to borrowers in the greatest financial need.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Student loan borrowers with older, high-rate loans

how_it_helps.text: It would refinance outstanding federal student loans — including older Direct Loans and FFEL bank-based loans — at the lower fixed interest rates that applied to loans issued for the year starting July 1, 2013, locking in the lower rate for the life of the loan.
It would let borrowers with private student loans convert them into federal loans at those lower federal rates, with eligibility rules aimed at borrowers with the greatest financial need.
Payments made on original loans would count toward income-based repayment and public-service repayment timelines, so refinancing would not reset the clock for borrowers pursuing forgiveness.

analysis.who_pays: Households with adjusted gross income above $1 million, who would pay a new minimum tax of 30% on income above that threshold (after charitable deductions) to fund the refinancing. Private student lenders would also lose interest revenue as borrowers refinanced out of their higher-rate loans, though they would be paid off in full.

drawbacks.text: The refinancing program was financed by a new 30% minimum tax on income above $1 million, a significant tax increase on high earners that opponents considered unfair or economically counterproductive.

Refinanced private loans would not qualify for public-service loan forgiveness or other loan-repayment and forgiveness programs, and only payments made after refinancing count toward income-based repayment timelines, making the deal worse than it appears for some borrowers.
Borrowers currently in default were excluded from private-loan refinancing, and the program was capped by a self-termination trigger tying its lifespan to estimated tax revenue, adding uncertainty.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side was real and immediate: millions of borrowers locked into pre-2013 rates would see fixed rates around 3.9% for undergraduates, saving hundreds to thousands of dollars a year, with eligibility rules targeting those in the most financial need. The main costs and objections: it was financed by a new minimum tax on millionaires, which critics opposed on tax-policy grounds and which could have modest economic effects; it paid private lenders off in full rather than imposing losses; the refinancing window was open-ended and capped only by a self-terminating spending trigger that could have proven hard to predict; and it gave refinanced private-loan borrowers fewer protections than direct-loan borrowers, while excluding borrowers currently in default. An honest supporter would also acknowledge that refinancing lowers payments without addressing why tuition keeps rising.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read the bill and sent it to the Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it expired when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015 without ever getting a floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 6, 2014, read twice, and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
The only further action was a hearing in a Banking Committee subpanel on June 4, 2014; the Finance Committee never reported the bill.
All 35 cosponsors were Democrats or allied independents, giving the bill little path past the Senate's 60-vote threshold even if it had reached the floor.
No vote was ever taken on the bill, and it died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student loan borrowers received no relief; high-income households avoided the new minimum tax, and private lenders kept their existing loan books at old rates.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led advocacy for student loan refinancing.

for.name: 35 senators (34 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Boxer, Murray, Durbin, Reed, Brown, Sanders, and others.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over the bill's tax provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action; the bill was never reported out of committee.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill to the floor for a vote during the 113th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 cosponsors were Democrats or an allied Independent, with no Republican support on record, and the bill never advanced out of the Finance Committee in a Senate controlled by Democrats but subject to a 60-vote floor threshold.

industries.note: The bill was paid for with a new 30% minimum tax on adjusted gross income above $1 million, net of charitable deductions. This was the direct cost imposed on the wealthiest households.
Private education lenders would lose borrowers who refinance into lower-rate federal loans, cutting their interest income. They would at least be paid off in full for the original loan.
The federal student loan program would collect less interest from refinanced loans, which is why the bill required a compensating new tax rather than adding to the deficit.
